text: This House would require social-media platforms to offer a non-algorithmic feed by default.
suggestedDefinitions: "Non-algorithmic" means a chronological feed of followed accounts; "by default" means users may still opt into ranking.
forContext: Defaults shape behaviour; chronological feeds return control and reduce engagement-optimised amplification.
againstContext: Ranked feeds surface relevance and safety filtering; a worse default may push users to noisier third-party apps.

text: This House believes smartphones should be banned during the school day.
suggestedDefinitions: "Banned" means stored away from first to last lesson, with medical exemptions.
forContext: Attention and social pressure improve when devices are out of reach; several school systems report calmer classrooms.
againstContext: Phones support safety, accessibility and digital literacy; enforcement costs may outweigh benefits.

text: This House would require AI-generated content to carry a visible label.
suggestedDefinitions: Applies to synthetic media presented as realistic; satire and obvious fiction may be exempted.
forContext: Labels preserve trust and informed judgement as synthetic media becomes indistinguishable.
againstContext: Labels are unenforceable at scale, punish honest creators and breed false confidence in unlabelled fakes.

text: This House would introduce a four-day working week as the national standard.
suggestedDefinitions: Standard full-time week becomes four days at reduced total hours, with sector-level flexibility.
forContext: Trials report stable productivity with better wellbeing and retention.
againstContext: Service and care sectors cannot compress output; costs fall unevenly on small employers.

text: This House would replace most welfare programmes with a universal basic income.
suggestedDefinitions: A flat unconditional payment to all adults, replacing means-tested cash benefits but not healthcare.
forContext: Universality removes poverty traps, stigma and administrative waste.
againstContext: Flat payments redirect money from the neediest and the fiscal arithmetic is demanding.

text: This House would tax frequent flying at sharply progressive rates.
suggestedDefinitions: A levy rising with each additional flight per person per year; first flight untaxed.
forContext: A small share of frequent flyers create most aviation emissions; progressive levies target them precisely.
againstContext: Mobility is a modern freedom; levies entrench privilege for those who can pay and punish diaspora families.
learningObjectives: Weigh climate impact against personal freedom

text: This House would lower the voting age to sixteen.
suggestedDefinitions: Applies to all national and local elections.
forContext: Sixteen-year-olds work, pay tax and inherit long-term policy outcomes; early voting builds lifelong habits.
againstContext: Cognitive and civic maturity arguments favour a consistent adulthood threshold.

text: This House would make voting compulsory.
suggestedDefinitions: Enforced with small fines, with a 'none of the above' ballot option.
forContext: Full turnout makes governments answer to everyone, not just motivated blocs.
againstContext: Forced participation is a rights violation and imports uninformed noise into results.

text: This House would impose term limits on all elected legislators.
suggestedDefinitions: A maximum of three terms in the same chamber.
forContext: Limits break incumbency advantage and career capture.
againstContext: Voters lose experienced representatives and power shifts to unelected staff and lobbyists.

text: This House believes universities should make standardised admissions tests optional.
suggestedDefinitions: Applicants choose whether to submit scores; other criteria are weighted accordingly.
forContext: Tests track family income and coaching more than potential.
againstContext: Without a common yardstick, admissions lean harder on essays and connections that favour privilege even more.

text: This House would pay students a stipend to complete secondary school.
suggestedDefinitions: A modest conditional cash transfer for attendance and completion.
forContext: Conditional transfers demonstrably raise completion where dropout is driven by family income pressure.
againstContext: Paying for attendance crowds out intrinsic motivation and spends scarce budget on those who would attend anyway.

text: This House would replace most written exams with project-based assessment.
suggestedDefinitions: Sustained coursework and portfolios replace timed papers as the main grade input.
forContext: Projects measure the sustained, collaborative work that adult life actually demands.
againstContext: Exams are the only assessment that is cheap, comparable and hard to outsource — especially in the AI era.

text: This House believes lying to protect someone's feelings is morally wrong.
suggestedDefinitions: Ordinary social falsehoods told to spare distress, not life-and-death deception.
forContext: Kind lies deny people accurate information about their own lives and corrode trust when discovered.
againstContext: Morality serves human wellbeing; gratuitous honesty is often cruelty in disguise.

text: This House would allow parents to select embryos for non-medical traits.
suggestedDefinitions: Selection among IVF embryos using polygenic screening for traits like height; germline editing excluded.
forContext: Parental freedom already governs schooling and upbringing; screening is a difference of degree.
againstContext: Trait markets entrench inequality and treat children as products; consent is impossible.

text: This House believes professional athletes are overpaid.
suggestedDefinitions: "Overpaid" means pay disproportionate to social contribution, not merely high.
forContext: Comparing athlete pay to nurses and teachers exposes a values gap markets ignore.
againstContext: Pay tracks the enormous, voluntary audience value athletes create in short careers.

text: This House would ban single-use plastics nationwide.
suggestedDefinitions: Prohibits sale of disposable plastic packaging and utensils with medical exemptions.
forContext: Bans shift producers to alternatives faster than voluntary pledges ever have.
againstContext: Substitutes often carry higher total footprints; bans hit the poor and disabled hardest.

text: This House would expand nuclear power as the core of the energy transition.
suggestedDefinitions: New-build reactors and lifetime extensions prioritised alongside renewables.
forContext: Nuclear delivers firm low-carbon baseload with tiny land use and a strong safety record per unit of energy.
againstContext: Costs and build times keep rising while renewables plus storage keep falling; capital is finite.

text: This House would give legal personhood to major rivers and forests.
suggestedDefinitions: Ecosystems gain standing to sue through appointed guardians, as pioneered in New Zealand.
forContext: Personhood forces courts to weigh nature's interests directly instead of via owners.
againstContext: Symbolic standing without enforcement budgets changes little and muddles liability.

text: This House would make permanent membership of the UN Security Council rotational.
suggestedDefinitions: Veto-holding seats rotate among regional blocs on fixed terms.
forContext: A 1945 power map cannot legitimately govern today's world.
againstContext: Great-power buy-in is the council's only currency; dilute it and powers exit the system.

text: This House believes rich nations should accept binding climate-migration quotas.
suggestedDefinitions: Treaty-based annual admissions proportional to historical emissions.
forContext: Causal responsibility for displacement implies a duty of remedy.
againstContext: Quotas politicise admissions, and adaptation funding helps far more people per dollar.

text: This House would ban sporting boycotts as a tool of international pressure.
suggestedDefinitions: International federations would bar states from withdrawing teams for political reasons.
forContext: Boycotts punish athletes, rarely change regimes and politicise the one arena built for peaceful contact.
againstContext: Sport is soft power; boycotts are among the few nonviolent levers ordinary nations hold.

text: This House would return all museum artefacts acquired under colonial rule.
suggestedDefinitions: Repatriation on request to origin states, with loan-back arrangements permitted.
forContext: Possession obtained under coercion cannot ripen into legitimate title.
againstContext: Universal museums preserve, research and display for everyone; unwinding history piecemeal invites endless claims.

text: This House believes streaming has made music better.
suggestedDefinitions: "Better" covers quality, diversity and access for listeners and artists.
forContext: Anyone can publish and anyone can listen; genres cross-pollinate at unprecedented speed.
againstContext: Per-stream economics push artists toward playlist-safe sameness and away from albums.

text: This House would fund national film industries through a tax on foreign streaming platforms.
suggestedDefinitions: A revenue levy on large foreign platforms earmarked for domestic production.
forContext: Platforms profit from national audiences while investing little in their stories.
againstContext: Levies raise subscription prices and invite retaliation; protected industries stagnate.

text: This House would ban junk-food sponsorship of professional sport.
suggestedDefinitions: Prohibits high-sugar and ultra-processed food brands from kits, stadia and broadcasts.
forContext: Sport's health halo is precisely why these brands buy it; the tobacco precedent worked.
againstContext: Sponsorship funds grassroots sport; the health effect of logo bans is speculative.

text: This House would allow athletes to compete under neutral flags whenever their federation is sanctioned.
suggestedDefinitions: Individual athletes may compete without national symbols while their federation is suspended.
forContext: Individuals should not carry collective punishment for federations they do not control.
againstContext: Neutral flags launder sanctioned states' prestige and blunt the only leverage sport has.

text: This House would require large companies to put workers on their boards.
suggestedDefinitions: Firms above 500 employees reserve a third of board seats for elected employees.
forContext: Codetermination aligns firms with long-term stability, as German experience suggests.
againstContext: Split boards slow hard decisions and blur accountability to owners.

text: This House believes founders should lose voting control when their companies go public.
suggestedDefinitions: Dual-class share structures sunset at IPO; one share, one vote thereafter.
forContext: Public capital deserves public accountability; entrenched founders answer to no one.
againstContext: Founder control shields long-term bets from quarterly markets — the very reason some iconic firms exist.

text: This House would make social-media platforms legally liable for algorithmically amplified content.
suggestedDefinitions: Liability attaches only where ranking actively promoted unlawful content, not mere hosting.
forContext: Amplification is an editorial act; publishers bear responsibility for what they promote.
againstContext: Liability at scale forces over-removal and entrenches incumbents who can afford compliance.

text: This House would fund public broadcasters through general taxation rather than licence fees.
suggestedDefinitions: Replace household licence fees with parliamentary budget allocations.
forContext: Licence fees are regressive and criminalise the poor; taxation is simpler and fairer.
againstContext: Budget dependence hands governments an annual lever over the newsroom that scrutinises them.

text: This House believes children should be paid for household chores.
suggestedDefinitions: Regular pocket money tied to completed tasks, distinct from unconditional allowance.
forContext: Payment teaches that effort earns reward and builds early money habits.
againstContext: Families run on mutual obligation, not wages; paying for chores commodifies belonging.

text: This House would ban homework in primary school.
suggestedDefinitions: No assigned at-home academic work before age eleven; reading encouraged.
forContext: Evidence for primary-age homework benefit is weak while family stress is real.
againstContext: Light homework builds routine and keeps parents connected to learning.
learningObjectives: Cite evidence at the right strength

text: This House believes remote work has been better for workers than for employers.
suggestedDefinitions: Compare aggregate gains since the remote-work shift across both groups.
forContext: Workers captured commute time, autonomy and geographic freedom.
againstContext: Employers cut real estate and hire globally; workers paid in blurred boundaries and stalled promotion.
